candidates.title: Don't add a blanket 'say N/A if impossible' hint to web agent prompts
candidates.rule: When prompting an LLM web agent on tasks that are mostly feasible, omit an explicit instruction to stop and answer 'N/A' when the task seems impossible; strong models still flag some infeasible tasks without it, and the hint causes premature give-ups on solvable tasks.
candidates.passage: eliminating this instruction led to a performance boost in achievable tasks, enhancing the overall task success rate of GPT-4 to 14.41%
candidates.finding: With the UA hint, GPT-4+CoT scored 11.70% overall (8.63% on achievable, 77.78% on unachievable) and misjudged 54.9% of feasible tasks as impossible. Removing the hint raised overall success to 14.41% and achievable success to 13.02%, while unachievable detection fell to 44.44%. GPT-3.5 without the hint detected only 8.33% of unachievable tasks and showed hallucination and action-repetition instead, so the trade-off is model-dependent.
workloads: WebArena (812 web tasks across shopping, Reddit/Postmill, GitLab, CMS, map, Wikipedia)
candidates.conditions: Two-shot in-context prompting, accessibility-tree observations with element IDs, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.9, max 30 state transitions, early stop on repeated or invalid actions.
candidates.limitations: Single paper, single benchmark; absolute success rates are very low (8-14%), so differences rest on few tasks. The benchmark has a minority of unachievable tasks; in deployments where refusing infeasible work matters more, the hint's recall benefit (77.78% vs 44.44% for GPT-4) may outweigh the achievable-task loss. No matched-cost or repeated-seed variance reported.
candidates.validation_test: Run your own agent on a task set with a known achievable/unachievable split, with and without the infeasibility hint, holding all else fixed; report success separately for achievable and unachievable tasks plus false-infeasible rate, over multiple seeds.

reason: The paper reports one clean prompt-level ablation (unachievable-task hint hurting achievable-task success for GPT-4) plus a validated LLM-as-judge fuzzy matching setup and an observation-representation design choice. The first two are actionable; the accessibility-tree choice is a design decision without a measured comparison, so it is not proposed.
